paragraphs.source_en: The role of pottery as an artistic and chronological indicator has been considered. Its rich decoration and excellent quality since the earliest dates suggest that the concept of "art" was already developed among huntergatherers producing it. As the pottery decoration is similar to the body decoration of the Round Head figures, a direct relationship seems plausible.

paragraphs.source_en: Two main typologies of painted sites were identified, namely open and hidden sites. The decisive criteria in such a distinction were their visibility in the landscape and their accessibility. The open sites consist of exposed shelters and panels visible from a large distance. The hidden sites, on the other hand, consist of shelters and panels hidden inside the surrounding rock outcrops, not immediately visible from outside and difficult to find. Although being so morphologically dissimilar, the two kinds of sites do not seem to present a different typology of paintings, indicating the general homogeneity of the painted themes.

paragraphs.source_en: The selection of sites was therefore motivated by reasons other than their being a good location for painting, and I hypothesize that it was for their different use. The places were used according to their function and the paintings were a product of those functions. According to the quantity and quality of paintings the highest mountain-range, the Tassili Plateau, appears to be the most significant area for the image-making. Only on this Plateau are all the characteristic elements present, whereas in the lower mountains of the Algerian Tadrart and the Tadrart Acacus only some of these elements are found. The Tassili Plateau also presents the greatest concentration of painted sites and panels, suggesting that the whole range was a major place of frequentation connected to the image-making.

paragraphs.source_en: For a better understanding and complete information about the Round Head art all painted sites must be considered and especially the previously neglected minor sites because their potential to inform is nevertheless great. In the sites all the panels must be studied and not just the most "interesting" ones, as was often practised in the previous research. The enormous potential of the landscape in the understanding of these paintings must be acknowledged and it opens a new direction for further research to undertake.
